opus-5.5.text:
I think of it as a shift in what success means.

In stage one, which for me was basically all of school and most of my early research years, the problem is handed to you. There's an exam, a homework set, a competition, a paper deadline. Someone has already decided the problem is worth solving, and your job is to solve it well and fast. Being good at that is valuable. It builds discipline, technical depth, and confidence. But it also trains a habit: you wait for the question, and you optimize hard against whatever metric you're given.

Stage two starts when nobody tells you what to do next. For me that became really clear during my PhD and especially when I started building Taichi. No advisor or reviewer could tell me, "This is the right problem, go solve it." I had to decide what was worth working on, why it mattered, and who it mattered to. That's a different skill. It's less about intelligence and more about taste, judgment, and being willing to own the consequences if you're wrong.

What surprised me is how uncomfortable that transition is. In stage one, feedback is quick and clear: you got the answer or you didn't. In stage two, feedback is slow and noisy. You can work on something for a year and still not know whether it was the right direction. A lot of very capable people get stuck there. They keep looking for the next external task, the next ranking, because that's where they know how to win.

So for me the transition meant a few things. First, I had to build my own sense of what problems are important, not just what's solvable or publishable. Second, I had to get comfortable with ambiguity and with being wrong in public. And third, I had to learn that defining the problem well is often more than half the work. If you choose the right problem, even an ordinary solution can have a big impact. If you choose the wrong one, the most brilliant solution doesn't matter much.

I don't think stage one is bad. It gives you the tools. But at some point you have to put the tools to use on questions you chose yourself. That's when the work starts to feel like yours.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the clearest way to put it is that in stage one, the hardest part of any problem has already been done for you, and you don't even realize it. When I was a PhD student at MIT, or even earlier doing competitive programming, someone handed me a well-defined problem. My advisor would say, here's a direction, here's why it matters, go figure out how to make it work. And I was good at that. You optimize, you grind, you make the thing faster or the paper better. The metric is given, and you climb it.

Stage two is when nobody hands you the metric anymore. When we started Taichi, and then later built the company around it, I remember the strange feeling of waking up and realizing that if I didn't decide what mattered today, nothing would happen. No one was going to tell me whether to focus on compiler performance, or developer experience, or talking to users, or hiring. All of those were plausibly correct. That's actually the scary part. In stage one, the wrong answers are usually obviously wrong. In stage two, almost every option looks reasonable, and you only find out years later which ones were.

So the transition is less about learning new skills and more about unlearning a habit, which is waiting for validation before you move. In school, if you do good work, someone tells you. In stage two, the feedback loop is slow and noisy, and sometimes the market tells you something completely different from what the smartest people around you say. You have to build your own internal compass and trust it enough to act, while staying honest enough to update when reality disagrees.

One thing that helped me was realizing that setting direction is itself a skill you can practice, not a personality trait you either have or don't. You can start small. Pick a problem no one assigned you, define success yourself, hold yourself to it, and see what happens. The first few times you'll probably choose badly, and that's fine. The point is to get comfortable with the discomfort of owning the question, not just the answer. I think a lot of technically strong people stall at this boundary, not because they can't execute, but because they never gave themselves permission to decide what's worth executing.

r001.rationale: It contrasts optimizing against a given metric in stage one with deciding what matters and what is worth executing in stage two.

r002.rationale: The response describes choosing priorities for oneself and a company, but does not state a shift from responsibility for one's own work to deciding what the whole team should do.

r003.rationale: It mentions an advisor assigning a direction, but does not say firsthand graduate research reveals important problems the advisor fails to recognize.

r004.rationale: It says technically strong people may stall at the transition, but does not state that greater success in stage one makes the transition more painful.

r005.rationale: It says stage two lacks a given metric and lists compiler performance as one possible priority, but does not clearly identify the absence of a defined efficiency metric as an obstacle to pursuing efficiency.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest change is that you go from solving a problem to deciding which problem is worth solving. In stage one, someone gives you a task, and usually there’s a relatively clear standard for doing it well. You can work very hard and get better at meeting that standard.

In stage two, the hard part is that nobody can give you that certainty. You have to ask yourself: What do I actually care about? Why is this worth my time? And if I spend several years on it, what would make that effort meaningful?

That transition can be uncomfortable, because being good at completing tasks doesn’t automatically mean you know how to choose a direction. I think you learn by trying things, making decisions, and reflecting on the results. You don’t need a perfect plan at the beginning, but you do need to take responsibility for choosing—and be willing to change your mind as you learn.

sol-6.1.text:
I think in stage one, the goal is usually given to you. A teacher gives you a problem, or someone tells you what to build, and your job is to solve it well. You can be very creative in how you solve it, but you don’t necessarily question whether that’s the right problem.

In stage two, choosing the problem becomes part of your responsibility. What is worth doing? Why does it matter? And why should you be the person to do it? There isn’t a standard answer or someone who can always tell you whether you’re on track.

That transition can be uncomfortable, because being good at completing tasks doesn’t automatically mean you know how to choose a direction. You have to try things, make judgments with incomplete information, and learn from what happens. To me, the important shift is taking ownership of the goal, as well as the work needed to reach it.
